generate.help.prompt.title: Prompt
generate.help.prompt.body: A plain description of what you want to see: the subject first, then where it is and how it looks. Concrete nouns and adjectives carry the weight, and anything you leave unsaid is filled in from whatever the model saw most of.
generate.help.negative.title: Negative prompt
generate.help.negative.body: A second prompt naming what to steer away from. It conditions the image in the opposite direction rather than acting as a quality switch, so it does most for you as a short list of things you do not want in frame.
generate.help.prompt_emphasis.title: Word emphasis
generate.help.prompt_emphasis.body: Writing part of a prompt as (a phrase:1.2) changes how hard it pulls. Just either side of 1 is a nudge, and past about 1.5 the phrase starts taking the rest of the picture apart.
generate.help.size.title: Width & height
generate.help.size.body: The size the image is drawn at rather than a crop of something larger, so changing it changes the picture. The preset chips set both sides at once, and a larger image costs more time and kudos.
generate.help.native_resolution.title: Native resolution
generate.help.native_resolution.body: Every model was trained at a size: around 512 a side for Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 1024 for SDXL. Ask for much less and you get a worse picture rather than a smaller one, with the subject cramped or gone.
generate.help.oversize.title: Going past native size
generate.help.oversize.body: Ask a model for much more than its native size and it repeats what it knows rather than filling the space: a second head, a third arm, a skyline that tiles. Hires fix is the way around it.
generate.help.steps.title: Steps
generate.help.steps.body: How many denoising passes the model makes. More steps can add detail but cost more time and kudos, and most models stop improving somewhere between 20 and 40.
generate.help.cfg.title: Guidance (CFG)
generate.help.cfg.body: How strictly the model is pushed to follow your prompt. Low values wander off it, high values look over-baked (hard edges, burnt colour); 5 to 10 suits most models, while distilled ones such as Flux Schnell want 1 or 2.
generate.help.sampler.title: Sampler
generate.help.sampler.body: The algorithm that turns noise into an image. Samplers differ in speed and character rather than in quality, and k_euler or k_dpmpp_2m are safe starting points.
generate.help.karras.title: Karras sigmas
generate.help.karras.body: Spaces the sampler's noise levels using the Karras schedule. It often sharpens results at low step counts, and some models are trained expecting it while others are not.
generate.help.hires.title: Hires fix
generate.help.hires.body: Renders at the model's native size first, then upscales and refines that image. It is the usual cure for the duplicated limbs and repeated subjects you get when a small model is asked for a large image.
generate.help.tiling.title: Tiling
generate.help.tiling.body: Makes the edges of the image wrap, so copies of it laid side by side join without a seam. Worth turning on for backgrounds, fabrics and ground textures, and of no use for a picture you are only going to look at once. The examples show one render repeated nine times beside the tile on its own, because a seam only exists where one copy meets the next.
generate.help.hires_denoise.title: Hires denoise
generate.help.hires_denoise.body: How much the second pass may repaint the upscaled image. Lower keeps the first pass's composition, higher lets the model add detail and drift from it.
generate.help.denoise.title: Denoising strength
generate.help.denoise.body: How much of your source image the model repaints. Low values stay close to the original, and near 1 almost nothing of it survives.
generate.help.clip_skip.title: CLIP skip
generate.help.clip_skip.body: Stops reading your prompt this many layers before the end of the text encoder. 1 is standard; many anime-derived models are trained for 2.
generate.help.seed.title: Seed
generate.help.seed.body: The number the image's starting noise is generated from. The same seed with the same settings reproduces the same image. Leave it blank for a fresh random one each time, and only fix it once you have a picture you like and want to change one thing about.
generate.help.loras.title: LoRAs & embeddings
generate.help.loras.body: LoRAs are small add-on files that pull a model toward a character, style, or concept, and textual inversions do the same through a prompt token. Strength scales how hard each one pulls, and a worker has to be able to fetch it before it can serve your request.
generate.help.upscaler.title: Upscaler
generate.help.upscaler.body: Enlarges the finished image with an upscaling model. It runs after generation, so it costs extra time and kudos but does not change the composition.
generate.help.facefixer.title: Face fix
generate.help.facefixer.body: Runs a face restoration model over the result. GFPGAN and CodeFormers repair small or distorted faces, at the cost of a little extra time.
generate.help.facefixer_strength.title: Face fix strength
generate.help.facefixer_strength.body: How strongly the face fixer is applied. It only reaches the request when a face fixer is selected, and high values clean up more but can make every face look alike.
generate.help.batch.title: Batch count
generate.help.batch.body: How many images this request asks for. Each one is charged its own kudos and shares your settings apart from the seed.
generate.help.transparent.title: Transparent background
generate.help.transparent.body: Asks for an image with a transparent background rather than a painted one. It needs a model and worker that support it, and it is not the same as the “Remove background” post-processor, which cuts the subject out afterwards.
generate.help.qr.title: QR code
generate.help.qr.body: Weaves a scannable QR code carrying this text or URL into the image. It needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5 or SDXL model, and these requests are never batched, so each image is queued on its own.
generate.help.webhook.title: Webhook URL
generate.help.webhook.body: An http(s) address the horde POSTs each finished generation to, for automation. Leave it blank if you are only using this page; an address that does not parse is dropped from the request rather than failing it.
generate.help.workers.title: Worker targeting
generate.help.workers.body: Pins the request to named workers, or in avoid mode keeps those workers off it. At most five IDs are accepted, and a short list usually means a longer wait.
generate.help.remember_extras.title: Remembering extras
generate.help.remember_extras.body: Keeps the webhook URL and worker list in this browser between visits. Turn it off if you would rather they reset when you reload.
generate.help.trusted_workers.title: Trusted workers
generate.help.trusted_workers.body: Restricts the request to workers the horde has marked as trusted. Far fewer workers qualify, so expect a longer wait in exchange for the tighter guarantee.
generate.help.slow_workers.title: Slow workers
generate.help.slow_workers.body: Lets slower workers pick the request up. Leaving it on usually gets you an image sooner; turning it off costs more kudos and favours faster hardware.
generate.help.extra_slow_workers.title: Extra slow workers
generate.help.extra_slow_workers.body: Also allows the slowest workers on the network. It can rescue an unpopular model that nothing else is running, at the cost of a long generation.
generate.help.allow_downgrade.title: Allow downgrade
generate.help.allow_downgrade.body: Lets the horde quietly reduce the request, for example to fewer steps, when you cannot afford its full kudos cost, instead of refusing it.
generate.help.replacement_filter.title: Prompt filtering
generate.help.replacement_filter.body: Lets the horde replace words its filters flag rather than reject the request. Turning it off means a flagged prompt fails outright instead.
generate.help.nsfw.title: NSFW
generate.help.nsfw.body: Marks the request as possibly not safe for work, so only workers that accept NSFW jobs pick it up. Leaving it off for an NSFW prompt risks the job being rejected.
generate.help.censor_nsfw.title: Censor NSFW
generate.help.censor_nsfw.body: Asks workers to return a censored placeholder if the result trips their NSFW detector, rather than the image itself.
generate.help.source.title: Source image modes
generate.help.source.body: How an attached image is used: img2img repaints it, ControlNet takes its structure (edges, depth, pose) as guidance, inpainting only repaints what you mask, and remix blends it with extra images on Stable Cascade models.
generate.help.requirements.title: Model suggestions
generate.help.requirements.body: Lines marked “Suggested” come from the selected model's own reference entry. They are recommendations rather than limits: a value the model was not tuned for is flagged, but the request is still sent as you set it.

generate.reference.quality_negative: Steers away from what you name; it is not a quality switch
generate.reference.quality_prompt_emphas: Past about 1.5 the weighted phrase starts taking the picture apart
generate.reference.quality_size: The shape changes the composition; area past native adds no detail
generate.reference.quality_oversize: One pass past native repeats the subject rather than enlarging it
generate.reference.quality_steps: Past the point a model settles, more is not better
generate.reference.quality_cfg: Too low wanders off the prompt, too high looks over-baked
generate.reference.quality_sampler: Changes the character of the image rather than its quality
generate.reference.quality_karras: Often sharper at low step counts
generate.reference.quality_hires_fix: Cures duplicated subjects at large sizes
generate.reference.quality_upscaler: Bigger, not different: the composition is already fixed
generate.reference.quality_facefixer: Repairs small faces, at the cost of what made them particular
generate.reference.prompt.lead: What you want to see, written as a plain description.
generate.reference.prompt.body: Your words are encoded and handed to the model on every pass rather than read once at the start, so the whole prompt pulls the whole way. That is why order matters: terms near the front pull hardest, and a description that opens with its subject gets a picture of that subject. A workable order is the subject, then the attributes that make it particular, then where it is, then how it was made: “a red fox asleep on a mossy log, morning light, 35mm photograph”. Concrete nouns and adjectives get further than mood words, because the model learned what a mossy log looks like and never learned what “epic” looks like. Anything you do not say is filled in from whatever it saw most of, so an unstated background, lens or palette is not neutral, it is that model's habit. Which model you are on decides those habits, which is why one prompt reads differently across two checkpoints.
generate.reference.negative.lead: A second prompt naming what the model should steer away from.
generate.reference.negative.body: It is conditioning in the opposite direction, applied on the same passes as the prompt, so it is a second pull rather than a filter over the result. Two things it does well. The first is naming the failure you keep getting: anatomy is what usually gives, and hands most of all, which is what the first strip steers. The second is taking out something you asked for by implication, which is the second strip: name the airships and they leave, and the skyharbor they were moored in stays. What it does badly is stand in for a quality setting. An inherited list of words like “bad, ugly, worst quality” pulls away from nothing in particular, and a term that has no counterpart in your prompt has nothing to pull against. Keep it short and specific, and add to it when you can point at what you are removing. Guidance scales the gap between the two prompts, so the same negative bites harder at 10 than at 3.
generate.reference.prompt_emphasis.lead: Weights that change how hard one part of your prompt pulls.
generate.reference.prompt_emphasis.body: Write a phrase as (a phrase:1.2) and it is weighted by that number. 1 is what the phrase would do with no parentheses at all, below 1 makes it a hint, above 1 makes it lead, and a nudge is usually all a style token needs. The first strip walks one style phrase from 0.5 to 2 and shows where the useful range ends: by 1.5 the washes are winning and the structure is going, and at 2 the phrase has taken the picture apart. The second strip is the half a single gradient cannot show. Two phrases are held in one prompt, winter and summer, and traded against each other across the strip; neither is ever removed, and the picture lands wherever the ratio puts it. That is what a weight is: a balance between the things you asked for rather than a volume control on each. Reach for it when one part of a prompt is being ignored or is dominating, and reach for plainer wording first when the whole thing is being read loosely.
generate.reference.size.lead: How large the picture is drawn, and which way round.
generate.reference.size.body: Width and height are the canvas the model paints on rather than a crop of something larger, so changing them changes the picture instead of the framing of one you already have. Each side moves in steps of 64, between 64 and 3072. The preset chips set the pair at once and are cut for the selected model's family, which is why the same “portrait 2:3” chip reads 512×768 on a Stable Diffusion 1.5 model and 832×1216 on an SDXL one. The shape matters as much as the area: a tall frame invites a standing figure and a wide one invites a landscape, and one prompt will compose itself differently in each. Area is what costs, because the work is counted in megapixelsteps, so doubling both sides quadruples the bill. Which sizes a given model is any good at is a separate question, answered under [[set:native_resolution]].
generate.reference.native_resolution.lea: The size a model was trained at, which is the size it knows a whole scene at.
generate.reference.native_resolution.bod: Training happened at a fixed size and the model's competence is built around it: around 512 a side for Stable Diffusion 1.5 and its descendants, and 1024 for SDXL. It is not a minimum or a recommendation so much as the scale at which the model knows what a whole scene looks like. The strip walks one SDXL request down from its native 1024 and the result is not a smaller version of the same picture. At 512 the anatomy holds but the framing collapses to a cramped close-up of whatever fits; at 256 the scene survives and the subject has gone; at 128 there is nothing left to read. Going the other way breaks differently, by repetition rather than by loss, which is what [[set:oversize]] covers. The panel knows both native squares and says so: it snaps an untouched size across when you switch to a model of the other family, and notes when your dimensions have drifted out of the one you are on. A moderate departure is fine, and every aspect preset is a moderate departure. It is the octave-sized ones that cost you the picture.
generate.reference.oversize.lead: What goes wrong when you ask for a picture much larger than the model's native size.
generate.reference.oversize.body: One pass over a large canvas does not give the model more room for the same scene, it gives it more room to repeat what it knows. Past the size it was trained at it no longer has a sense of what a whole body or a whole composition looks like at that scale, so it paints several: a second head, a third arm, a skyline that tiles. That is why a picture that is wrong at 1536 is often exactly right at 1024. Stable Diffusion 1.5 models start showing it past about 768 on a side and the panel says so on the size control; SDXL holds on further and then breaks the same way. There are two ways out and they are different tools. The hires pass generates at a size the model is competent at, then enlarges that image and repaints it, so the composition is decided where it can be decided well. An upscaler runs afterwards on the finished picture, which makes it bigger without making it different. Neither is a reason to avoid large images: they are the reason large images work.
generate.reference.loras.lead: LoRAs and textual inversions are small add-on files that pull a model towards a character, a style or a concept.
generate.reference.loras.body: A LoRA is loaded alongside the checkpoint and nudges what it paints; a textual inversion does the same through a token you put in the prompt. Each carries a strength, and for a LoRA the model and CLIP strengths scale how hard it pulls on the picture and on the prompt reading. Around 1 is the usual starting point, and pushing far past it tends to flatten everything else the model knows. A worker has to be able to fetch the file before it can serve your request, so an obscure add-on can leave the job waiting.
generate.reference.source.lead: Says how an image you attach is used: repainted, read for its structure, masked, or blended.
generate.reference.source.body: img2img repaints the whole picture, keeping as much of it as the denoising strength allows. ControlNet takes the structure out of it (edges, depth, a pose) and paints something new on that skeleton, so the composition survives and little else does. Inpainting repaints only the area you mask and leaves the rest untouched. Remix blends your image with a handful of extra ones, and only Stable Cascade models serve it.
generate.reference.denoise.lead: How much of your source image the model is allowed to repaint.
generate.reference.denoise.body: At low values the result is your picture with a light pass over it; near 1 almost nothing of the original survives. The middle is where img2img usually earns its place: enough freedom to change the style or the light, not so much that the subject moves. It applies to img2img, ControlNet and inpainting alike. Remix weights its inputs per image instead, and ignores this. It belongs to requests that start from an image: on a plain text prompt leave it at 1, because a lower value quietly cuts steps off the end of the schedule, and a few-step model like Flux Schnell comes back as a washed-out, noise-flecked sketch. The strip comes in two readings, on an ancestral sampler and on one that settles: an ancestral sampler re-rolls detail as the strength rises, so some of what moves along that strip is the sampler rather than the strength, and the settling reading is how you tell the two apart.
generate.reference.steps.lead: How many denoising passes the model makes on its way from noise to a picture.
generate.reference.steps.body: Each pass refines what the last one left, so more steps can mean more detail, and each one costs time and kudos. Most models stop improving somewhere between 20 and 40, and past that you are usually paying for a picture nobody can tell from the cheaper one. How fast a model gets there depends on the sampler as much as on the model: some settle towards a single image, and some re-roll the detail at every count. Where a model's reference entry suggests a range, the panel marks it on the steps control.
generate.reference.cfg.lead: How strictly the model is pushed to follow your prompt.
generate.reference.cfg.body: Low values let it wander off the prompt and invent; high values force every word in and tend to look over-baked, with hard edges and burnt colour. Between 5 and 10 suits most models. Distilled models are the exception, and Flux Schnell and its relatives want 1 or 2. Guidance and steps read against each other, so a value that works at 30 steps may not at 10.
generate.reference.sampler.lead: The algorithm that turns the starting noise into an image.
generate.reference.sampler.body: Samplers differ in character and in how quickly they converge rather than in quality, and there is no best one. k_euler and k_dpmpp_2m are safe starting points. The choice that matters most for the rest of the panel is whether your sampler settles or re-rolls. A settling sampler walks steadily towards one image, so raising the steps refines the picture you were already getting and the gain tails off once it has arrived. A re-rolling sampler stirs a little fresh noise back in on every pass, so it never quite arrives: raise the steps and you get a different picture rather than a cleaner version of the same one, which is why a step count that suited one of these may look unfinished at another. Neither behaviour is a fault, but it decides whether it is worth paying for more steps. The naming is a reliable hint: an _a suffix marks an ancestral sampler and sde marks a stochastic one, and both re-roll. In full, the re-rollers are k_euler_a, k_dpm_2_a, k_dpmpp_2s_a and k_dpmpp_sde; the settlers are k_euler, k_dpm_2, k_dpmpp_2m, k_heun, k_lms, DDIM, dpmsolver and lcm. Some models name the samplers they were tuned for, and the panel marks those as suggested.
generate.reference.seed.lead: The number the image's starting noise is generated from.
generate.reference.seed.body: The same seed with the same settings and the same model gives the same image every time, which is what makes it possible to change one setting and see only that change. Leave it blank and the horde picks a fresh random seed for each request, which is the normal way to work: you fix the seed once you have a picture you like and want to change one thing about it. Each image in a batch shares your settings apart from the seed, so a batch is variations rather than copies.
generate.reference.clip_skip.lead: Stops reading your prompt this many layers before the end of the text encoder.
generate.reference.clip_skip.body: The encoder builds meaning up in layers, and stopping early hands the model a looser, less literal reading of what you asked for. 1 is standard and is what most models were trained against. Many anime-derived checkpoints were trained at 2, and on those the difference is not subtle. Where a model states a value, the panel marks it on the CLIP skip control as a suggestion.
generate.reference.karras.lead: Spaces the sampler's noise levels using the Karras schedule instead of the default one.
generate.reference.karras.body: The schedule decides how much noise comes off at each step rather than how many steps there are. Karras spends more of them at the low-noise end, which often sharpens the result at low step counts and matters less as the count rises. Some models are trained expecting it and some are not, and the panel reads the model's suggested schedulers to say which. The horde's own default is off; this form starts it on.
generate.reference.hires.lead: Renders at the model's native size first, then upscales that image and refines it.
generate.reference.hires.body: Asking a model for a picture much larger than it was trained on is what produces two heads and three legs: at that scale it no longer knows what a whole body looks like, so it paints several. The hires pass sidesteps this by generating small, where the model is competent, and repainting the enlarged version. It costs a second pass of time and kudos. The panel suggests it when a Stable Diffusion 1.5 model is asked for more than 768 pixels on either side.
generate.reference.hires_denoise.lead: How much the hires pass is allowed to repaint the upscaled image.
generate.reference.hires_denoise.body: The second pass starts from the enlarged first render rather than from noise, and this decides how much of it survives. Low values keep the first pass's composition and mostly add sharpness; high values let the model add detail that was never there, and drift from the picture you were enlarging. It only reaches the request while the hires pass is on.
generate.reference.tiling.lead: Makes the edges of the image wrap, so copies laid side by side join without a seam.
generate.reference.tiling.body: The model is asked to paint something whose left edge continues into its right and whose top continues into its bottom. That is worth having for backgrounds, fabrics, ground textures and anything else meant to repeat, and of no use for a picture you are only going to look at once. It constrains the composition, so it is not free. The examples show one render repeated nine times beside the tile on its own, because a seam only exists where one copy meets the next.
generate.reference.requirements.lead: The lines marked “Suggested” under a control come from the selected model's own reference entry.
generate.reference.requirements.body: Model authors publish the steps, guidance, samplers, schedulers and CLIP skip their checkpoint was tuned for, and the panel shows those beside the fields they apply to. They are recommendations rather than limits. A value the model was not tuned for is flagged, and the request is still sent exactly as you set it. A model that publishes nothing shows no lines at all, which is not a statement that any value will do.
generate.reference.upscaler.lead: Enlarges the finished image with a dedicated upscaling model.
generate.reference.upscaler.body: It runs after generation, on the picture the model produced, so it changes nothing about the composition and cannot rescue a bad one. The plain and anime variants of RealESRGAN suit photographic and drawn work respectively. At most one upscaler runs, so picking a second replaces the first. It is a different tool from the hires pass, which enlarges mid-generation and repaints as it goes.
generate.reference.facefixer.lead: Runs a face restoration model over the result.
generate.reference.facefixer.body: Small faces are where generation falls apart first: at a distance there are not enough pixels for the model to place eyes and a mouth convincingly. GFPGAN and CodeFormers rebuild them from what a face is generally supposed to look like. That is also the catch, because what they know is faces in general rather than the one in your picture. It does nothing for a face that is already large and correct.
generate.reference.facefixer_strength.le: How strongly the face fixer is applied.
generate.reference.facefixer_strength.bo: Low values are a touch-up and the original face still shows through; high values rebuild more of it, which clears up more damage and can leave every face in a batch looking related. It only reaches the request when a face fixer is actually selected, so moving it on its own does nothing.
generate.reference.batch.lead: How many images this one request asks for.
generate.reference.batch.body: Each image is charged its own kudos and shares every setting apart from the seed, so a batch shows you several readings of one prompt rather than several prompts. That makes it the quickest way to find out whether a prompt is working, because one bad seed is not evidence. QR-code requests are never batched, and each image in them is queued on its own.
generate.reference.nsfw.lead: Marks the request as possibly not safe for work, so only workers that accept those jobs pick it up.
generate.reference.nsfw.body: It is a declaration about the request rather than a filter on the result. Leaving it off for a prompt that is plainly NSFW risks the job being rejected by a worker that did not sign up for it. Turning it on narrows the pool of workers willing to take the job, which can mean a longer wait.
generate.reference.censor_nsfw.lead: Asks workers to return a censored placeholder if the result trips their NSFW detector.
generate.reference.censor_nsfw.body: The check happens on the worker after the image has been generated, so this decides what comes back rather than what is made. It is on by default. It is a separate question from the NSFW flag, which is about which workers are willing to take the job at all: a request can be marked NSFW and still ask for a censored return.
generate.reference.trusted_workers.lead: Restricts the request to workers the horde has marked as trusted.
generate.reference.trusted_workers.body: Trust is earned by workers that have served a great deal of correct work, so the trusted pool is a small fraction of the network. That is the whole trade: a tighter guarantee about who runs your prompt, against a queue that can be much longer. It is off by default, which is the right setting for almost everything.
generate.reference.slow_workers.lead: Lets slower workers pick the request up.
generate.reference.slow_workers.body: It is on by default, and leaving it on usually gets you an image sooner, because more machines can take the job. Turning it off holds the request to faster hardware and costs more kudos for the same picture. Turn it off when you are waiting on something and want it now; leave it on the rest of the time.
generate.reference.extra_slow_workers.le: Also allows the slowest workers on the network to take the request.
generate.reference.extra_slow_workers.bo: These are the machines that would otherwise be filtered out entirely. It is worth turning on for an unpopular model that nothing else on the network is running, where a slow result beats no result. Expect the generation itself to take a long time. It is off by default.
generate.reference.allow_downgrade.lead: Lets the horde quietly reduce the request rather than refuse it when you cannot afford its full cost.
generate.reference.allow_downgrade.body: The reduction lands on the settings that carry the cost, such as the step count, so what comes back is a cheaper version of what you asked for rather than nothing at all. It is on by default, which suits anyone who would rather have an image than an error. Turn it off when you need the settings you set to be the settings that ran.
generate.reference.replacement_filter.le: Lets the horde replace words its filters flag instead of rejecting the whole request.
generate.reference.replacement_filter.bo: The horde runs prompts through filters, and this decides what happens when one fires: with it on the flagged wording is swapped and the request goes through, and with it off the request fails outright. It is on by default, here and on the horde's side. Turning it off is a way of being told that a prompt was flagged, rather than wondering why the result did not match it.
generate.reference.webhook.lead: An http(s) address the horde POSTs each finished generation to.
generate.reference.webhook.body: It is for automation: a script or service of your own that would rather be told when an image is ready than poll for it. Leave it blank if you are only using this page. An address that does not parse as an http or https URL is dropped from the request rather than failing it, so a typo costs you the callback and nothing else.
generate.reference.workers.lead: Pins the request to named workers, or in avoid mode keeps those workers off it.
generate.reference.workers.body: At most five worker IDs are accepted. A short list usually means a longer wait, because only the machines on it can serve the request and they may be busy or offline. Avoid mode is the more useful half for most people: it routes around one worker that has been giving you bad results without narrowing the pool to almost nothing.
generate.reference.remember_extras.lead: Keeps the webhook URL and the worker list in this browser between visits.
generate.reference.remember_extras.body: Both carry account-shaped detail, so they are session-only unless you ask for them to be kept: reload with this off and they are blank again. Everything else in the panel is remembered either way, including the QR text. Turn it on if you send every generation to the same webhook.
generate.reference.transparent.lead: Asks for an image with a transparent background rather than a painted one.
generate.reference.transparent.body: The transparency is produced during generation, so the edges are decided by the model as it paints rather than cut out afterwards. It needs a model and a worker that support it, and comes back opaque where they do not. It is not the same thing as the “Remove background” post-processor, which takes a finished image and cuts the subject out of it.
generate.reference.qr.lead: Weaves a scannable QR code carrying this text or URL into the image itself.
generate.reference.qr.body: The code is part of the picture rather than pasted over it, so the prompt still decides what the image is of. Ask for weather, vapour, foliage and light rather than blocks and hard shadows: the ControlNet already carries the code, and a prompt that describes geometry competes with it for the same pixels. Beside the payload the request can carry where the code sits, in pixels from the left and top edge, and which shape its squares are drawn as; left alone, the workflow centres a square code. How hard the ControlNet holds the render to the code is a real dial in the renderer, and the public API has no field to carry it, so a job sent to the horde lands at the workflow's own baseline whatever it asks for. The strip on this page is that dial moved locally, and it is worth reading for what the range does rather than as something to set: on the horde, a code that scans is bought with the prompt and its texture instead. It needs a Stable Diffusion 1.5 or SDXL model. These requests are never batched, so each image in a batch is queued on its own. Leave the box blank and the workflow is not used at all.
generate.guide.title: The Generate page, explained
generate.guide.lead: The control panel builds one request, and the results pane shows what comes back. You only need the prompt box and the Generate button to start; every other card is there for when you want to steer the result.
generate.guide.steps.prompt.title: Describe what you want
generate.guide.steps.prompt.body: Type a plain description into the prompt box: what the subject is, where it is, and how it should look. Concrete nouns and adjectives carry most of the weight, so “a red fox asleep on a mossy log, morning light” gets further than a single word. The negative prompt box is for what you would rather not see.
generate.guide.steps.model.title: Pick a model, or a style
generate.guide.steps.model.body: A model is the network that draws the image. A style is a saved bundle of prompt wording, settings, and a model chosen to go with them, so picking one from Browse is the quickest way to a coherent look. Either is a fine start, and the defaults are a fine start too.
generate.guide.steps.dimensions.title: Choose a size
generate.guide.steps.dimensions.body: Width and height are the size the image is drawn at rather than a crop of something larger, so changing them changes the picture itself. Every model has a size it was trained at: around 512 for SD 1.5 models and 1024 for SDXL ones, and the presets in the Dimensions card set both at once. Ask a model for much less than it was trained on and you do not get a smaller version of the same picture, you get a worse one, with the subject cramped or gone entirely. Ask for much more and it tends to repeat things, which is what Hires fix is there to undo.
generate.guide.steps.generate.title: Send it to the horde
generate.guide.steps.generate.body: Press Generate. Your request joins a queue that volunteer workers pick up, so an image arrives in anything from a few seconds to a few minutes depending on how busy the network is and how rare the model is. The batch count next to Generate asks for several images at once.
generate.guide.steps.results.title: Read what came back
generate.guide.steps.results.body: Every finished image lands in the results pane as a tile. Open one for a larger view, and use its menu to reuse the settings that made it, send it back as a source image, or download it. Results are kept in this browser rather than on the horde, so download anything you want to keep.
generate.guide.steps.advanced.title: Then step into the settings
generate.guide.steps.advanced.body: Once an image is close but not right, the other cards in the panel are how you close the gap. Sampling decides how the image is drawn, the Source image card starts you from a picture instead of from noise, and Horde options decide who runs the job. Change one thing at a time, and keep the same seed if you want to compare like with like.

generate.learn.flows.concepts_images.ste: It starts as static

Drag the slider. At its start is the static every image starts as, a square of pure noise with nothing in it. Each notch along is one more pass of the model, asked the same question every time: what would this look like with a little less noise in it? Somewhere in the middle the shapes arrive, and by the far end the static has gone. Nothing was copied in from anywhere; every pixel came out of that guessing. The model's guess, offered as the second reading, is the finished picture it thought it was heading towards from each point along the way, which is why a half-done render is unfinished rather than random.

Generating is denoising. A field of random noise goes through the model repeatedly, each pass predicting some of the noise and subtracting it, until what is left is a picture. There is no canvas being painted on, and nothing is retrieved from a library.
Iterative denoising from a random latent: each step predicts noise and removes a scheduled fraction of it, so the image is the outcome of the process rather than anything stored.
The prompt steers every pass

Every pass you just scrubbed through was steered by your words. They are turned into numbers and handed to the model on each one, so they pull the whole way rather than being read once at the start. That is why a prompt reads as a pull rather than an instruction: words near the front pull harder, repeating or emphasising a word pulls harder still, and anything you never mention gets filled in from whatever the model thinks is usual. [[set:negative]] pulls the other way, naming what to steer away from.

The prompt is encoded and used as conditioning on every step, not read once at the start. Order and emphasis change the weighting, so terms near the front carry more, and anything unstated falls to the model's habits. [[set:negative]] conditions in the opposite direction.

Text conditioning is applied per step, so token position and emphasis shift the whole trajectory rather than a first guess; unstated attributes fall to the prior, which is what makes a negative worth writing.
What the model learned

The thing making all those guesses is a large file of numbers. It was shown millions of images with text describing them, and trained to undo noise added to them, which is the job you just watched it do. It does not keep the pictures. What it keeps is a sense of what things tend to look like: how skin catches light, how a bicycle is put together, how a photograph differs from an oil painting. Different [[gl:model|models]] were shown different sets of images, which is why each one has its own look and its own strengths.

A [[gl:model|model]] is weights, not a library. Training added noise to captioned images and taught the network to predict it, leaving a statistical sense of how things look rather than the images themselves. What it was trained on is why one model draws better faces and another better landscapes.
Weights fitted to predict noise over captioned data. The training set's leanings are the model's style, which is why the baseline and the finetune move a result further than any single setting does.
Steps and guidance

Two numbers govern the run you just watched. [[set:steps]] is how many passes it makes, and the strip for this step is the same picture at a handful of counts: too few and it stays vague, and past a point the extra passes cost time and [[gl:kudos|kudos]] without changing much. [[set:cfg]] is how hard the model is pushed to obey your words: too low and it wanders off somewhere prettier than what you asked for, too high and the colours go harsh and the picture looks over-baked. The settings reference in these Learn pages gives the workable range for each.

[[set:steps]] is the count of denoising passes; [[set:cfg]] is how tightly the result is held to your words. Too few steps leaves the image unresolved, and high guidance burns the contrast. The settings reference lists the workable range for both, with sweep strips beside them.

Steps sets the schedule length, CFG the gap between the conditioned and unconditioned predictions. Both have a knee past which you pay without gaining, which is why the settings reference gives ranges rather than one number.
Why the same prompt gives a different picture

The static you scrubbed back to at the start is generated from a number, and that number is [[set:seed]]. The same seed with the same model and settings gives the same image every time; a fresh seed gives a different picture from the same words, which is what the pictures here are, and which is why running a prompt again is a fair way to look for a better result. That is also why the seed is normally left blank, and fixed only once you have a picture you want to refine. [[set:sampler]] is the method used to walk through the passes, and some samplers add a little noise back as they go, so they keep varying where everything else is fixed. [[gl:worker|Workers]] across the horde also differ in hardware and software, so an exact match to someone else's image is not something to expect.

The starting noise comes from [[set:seed]]: fix it and a run reproduces, leave it blank and every submit re-rolls, which is the everyday setting. [[set:sampler]] is the method that walks the steps, and ancestral ones keep injecting noise, so detail moves when the step count does. Hardware and library versions differ between [[gl:worker|workers]] as well.
Seed fixes the initial latent, sampler fixes the path. Ancestral variants re-inject noise, so step count is not neutral there, and cross-worker determinism is not promised in any case.

generate.learn.flows.concepts_horde.step: People lending their graphics cards

There is no data centre behind this. The AI Horde is a crowd of volunteers running a small program called a worker on their own computers, which asks the horde for jobs and sends the results back. When you press Generate, someone's machine at home draws your picture. The number of workers rises and falls through the day as people switch them on and off, and so does the list of models you can pick from, because each worker chooses which models it carries.

The horde is a pool of volunteer-run workers rather than a hosted service. Each worker asks for jobs, generates, and returns the result. Capacity and the model list both move with who happens to be online, since workers choose what they carry.
A job broker over volunteer workers. Capacity and model availability track who is online, which is why the model list is fetched rather than fixed.
What happens after you press Generate

Your request goes into the horde's queue rather than to a particular machine. Workers ask for work as they free up, and one that carries your model and can meet what you asked for takes the job, generates the image, and sends it back for the horde to hand to you. Where you sit in that queue depends on your kudos and on how ordinary the request is: a common model at a common size is picked up sooner than something only a couple of workers can serve.

Submitting puts the request in a shared queue. Workers poll it, and one matching the model and the request's requirements claims the job, generates, and returns the image. Queue position follows your kudos and how many workers can serve the request at all.
The request enters a shared queue; workers claim by capability match. Ordering is by kudos, and the count of workers able to serve it sets the floor on how fast anything moves.
Kudos, and what they are not

Kudos are how the horde keeps track of who has given and who has taken. Running a worker and generating for other people earns them; asking for images spends them. They are not money and not a cryptocurrency: they cannot be bought, sold or cashed out, and they buy nothing outside the horde. What they do is set your place in the queue. You can generate with none of them, or with a negative balance, and without an account at all. It only means waiting behind the people who have contributed.

Kudos are contribution accounting: earned by generating for others, spent by asking for images. They are not a currency, cannot be traded, and buy nothing outside the horde. Their only effect is queue priority, so a low or negative balance costs you waiting rather than access.
A priority ledger, not a balance you can spend elsewhere. There is no exchange and no hard gate, so a negative balance costs latency and nothing else.
Trust and content flags

Because strangers' computers do the work, the horde keeps track of how far each worker has proved itself. Workers that have served reliably over time become trusted, and you can ask that only those handle your requests, which usually means waiting longer for a smaller pool. Every request also carries a flag saying whether it may come back with adult content, and workers set their own limits on what they will accept, so a request marked that way goes to the workers willing to serve it. Both are options in the panel rather than things to think about on your first image.

Workers earn trust by serving reliably, and you can restrict a request to trusted ones at the cost of a smaller pool and a longer wait. The NSFW flag on a request is matched against what each worker is willing to accept. Both live in the horde section of the panel.

Trust is earned over served jobs; restricting to trusted workers narrows the pool and costs latency. The NSFW flag is matched against per-worker limits, so it routes the job rather than filtering afterwards.
Why the wait moves around

Waits swing about a great deal, and it is worth knowing why rather than guessing. How many workers are online at that moment, how many people are queued ahead of you, how rare the model you picked is, and how much work your request is to run all feed into it. A large image with many steps takes a worker longer than a small one. Anyone quoting you a fixed number would be making it up; what you can do is watch the estimate the studio shows, and pick a common model when you are in a hurry.

The wait depends on how many workers are online, how deep the queue ahead of you is, how many workers carry your model, and how much work the request is (size and steps). None of that is fixed, so the studio shows an estimate rather than a promise, and a common model at a common size is the fastest thing to ask for.
Latency follows live worker count, queue depth ahead of you, model availability and the request's own cost. All four move, so the estimate is an estimate.
See it for yourself

None of this is hidden. The Workers page lists every machine signed in right now, what it carries and how much it has generated, and the Status page shows the queue and how much work the horde is getting through. If you have not made an image yet, the walkthrough takes one request through the panel field by field and ends with you sending it into the queue you have just been reading about.
The Workers page lists who is online and what they carry, and the Status page shows the current queue and throughput. The walkthrough takes one request through the panel and into that queue.
Workers and Status show the live pool and the queue. The walkthrough runs one committed request through the panel.
Make an image now
Coming from another tool
The panel speaks your language

If you have generated images in another program, most of this panel is already familiar. The prompt box and the negative prompt box are what you expect. Steps is steps. CFG is what some tools label guidance: how hard the model is pushed to obey your words. The sampler list holds the same names you have been picking from. Seed is the number the starting static comes from, and denoising strength, on a run that starts from a picture you supply, is how much of that picture survives. Two things have moved rather than been renamed. Hires fix is a switch with its own strength slider beside it rather than one control, and clip skip sits in the Sampling card rather than in a settings page of its own. The strips here show both of them changing, so you can check they behave the way you expect before you rely on them.

Your vocabulary carries over intact. Prompt and negative prompt, steps, CFG (guidance, in the tools that call it that), sampler, seed, and denoising strength on a sourced run all mean here what they mean everywhere else, and the sampler names are the k_ ones you already choose between. Two have moved. Hires fix is a toggle paired with its own denoising slider rather than a single control, and clip skip is a per-request field under Sampling rather than an application setting you set once. Both have strips here, so you can see them behaving as you would expect rather than take it on trust. Nothing else has been renamed, and every field's reference page names the API field behind it.

The same parameter set under the same names, with the API field on each reference page. Two to relearn: hires fix is a toggle plus a paired denoise, and clip skip is per-request under Sampling rather than an app-level setting.
What the horde changes

The real difference is where the work happens. None of your hardware is involved: the request goes to the AI Horde, a volunteer's computer somewhere picks it up, generates the image and sends it back. That is why there is no progress bar. Nothing is running on your machine to report on, so what you watch instead is your place in the queue and how fast the worker that claimed your job happens to be. The second new idea is kudos. They are how the horde keeps track of who has given and who has taken: running a worker for other people earns them, and asking for images spends them. They set your place in the queue rather than gating anything, so generating is free, and works with no kudos, a negative balance, or no account at all.

There is no fixed hardware behind this. Your request goes into a shared queue, a volunteer-run worker claims it, generates, and returns the result. So the local progress bar is replaced by two numbers that are not about your machine: where you sit in the queue, and how fast the worker that took the job is. Kudos are the other new idea, and they are contribution accounting rather than currency: earned by generating for others, spent by asking for images, not purchasable and not tradable. Their only effect is queue priority, so generating is free and a zero or negative balance costs you waiting rather than access, with or without an account.

A job broker over volunteer workers rather than a local runtime, so queue position and the claiming worker's throughput stand in for a progress bar. Kudos are a priority ledger, not a paywall: a low or negative balance costs latency and nothing else.
What to expect differently

Three habits are worth adjusting before they surprise you. First, a seed is not a promise. Fix it and the same worker will give you the same image, but the next worker runs different hardware and different library versions, so an exact match is not something to count on; the strip here is the larger effect, which is what a fresh seed does to the same prompt. Second, the model list is whatever the workers online at this moment are carrying, so a model you used yesterday can be missing this evening and back tomorrow. Third, some of the dials your old program had have no field here at all: custom schedulers, extension scripts and add-ons belong to that program, and a request sent to the horde has to be something any matching worker can run.

Three expectations to reset. Determinism is per-worker: the seed fixes the starting noise, but hardware and library versions vary across the pool, so reproducing someone else's image exactly is not something to plan around. The strip here is the ordinary case, the same request re-rolled. Model availability moves with the pool, because each worker chooses what it carries, so the list is fetched rather than fixed and a model can be absent for an evening. And parts of your renderer's surface have no API field at all, custom schedulers and extension scripts among them, since a request has to be servable by any worker that matches it. What the panel offers is the common ground, not a cut-down copy of one tool.

Cross-worker determinism is not promised: the seed fixes the latent, but hardware and library versions vary across the pool. Model availability tracks who is online. Anything outside the horde's request schema, extension scripts and bespoke schedulers included, has no field, because any matching worker has to be able to serve the payload.
The model list is a pool, not a folder

In a local program the model dropdown is your own folder of files, and it grows when you download something. Here it is a list of what the volunteers online are carrying between them, and it changes without you touching it. There is nothing to download and no disk space to manage. What is new is that the choice has a cost: a common model has many workers able to take your job, so it comes back sooner, while a rare one can mean a long wait or none at all. You also start further along on settings than you would locally. Each model has a reference entry saying what it was tuned for, and the panel passes that on, marking the sampler it suggests, whether it wants Karras sigmas, and the clip skip it was trained at, under the controls themselves.

The model picker is the horde's worker pool rather than a directory on disk: nothing to download, nothing to keep, and the list moves as workers come and go. That makes model choice a throughput decision as well as an aesthetic one, since a common model has more workers able to claim the job than a rare one. It also removes a round of trial and error you are probably used to doing yourself: models carry reference entries naming the sampler, schedule and clip skip they were tuned for, and the panel surfaces those as suggestions on the controls they apply to rather than leaving them to be found.

The list is the union of what online workers carry, so availability and queue depth are properties of the model you pick. Reference entries carry suggested sampler, schedule and clip skip, and the panel marks them inline.
Run one and see where it lands

That is the whole of the difference: the same controls under nearly the same names, someone else's machine doing the work, a queue in place of a progress bar, and a model list that belongs to the crowd rather than to you. The quickest way to settle the rest is to send one request. The walkthrough takes a real one through the panel field by field and ends with you pressing Generate, and you can move past any step whose field you already know.

alchemy.usecases.head: What Alchemy is for
alchemy.usecases.lead: Alchemy works on a picture you already have. Its twenty-four operations do four things between them, and every one of them starts from an image you supply.
alchemy.usecases.describe.title: Describe a picture
alchemy.usecases.describe.note: Ask the horde what is in an image. These operations answer with text or data rather than with a new picture, with the one exception noted on the page.
alchemy.usecases.describe.lead: Reads an image and answers with words, tags or numbers instead of another image.
alchemy.usecases.describe.body: Every form here takes the same source and returns something you can read or store: a one-line caption, a tag list, a safety verdict, a colour palette. Several can run on one submission, so a single upload can come back captioned, tagged and rated at once. The control map is the odd one out: it also answers a question about the picture, but it answers in an image, and the studio does not offer it as an operation.
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.title: Enlarge a picture
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.note: Run an upscaler over the image. Which one to pick depends on whether the source is a photograph, artwork or animation.
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.lead: Redraws the image at two or four times its size, filling in detail the original never had.
alchemy.usecases.enlarge.body: An upscaler is a model, and what it was trained on decides what it invents in the gaps. The photographic models keep skin and fabric plausible, while the anime models keep line art crisp instead of smearing it into gradients. The badge on each row is the factor that model enlarges by. Vectorize is filed here without a badge because it answers the same wish differently: it redraws the picture as shapes, and an SVG has no resolution to run out of.
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.title: Repair faces
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.note: Rebuild faces a generator got wrong. Most useful on small or distant faces, which is where models fail first.
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.lead: Finds faces in the image and redraws them, which is the usual repair for the melted features small renders produce.
alchemy.usecases.fix_faces.body: GFPGAN restores heavily and will happily replace a face that was nearly right; CodeFormers keeps more of the original and is the safer choice on a portrait you mostly like. Running either over a face that was already correct still changes it, so this is a repair rather than a finishing pass.
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.title: Cut out the background
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.note: Remove everything behind the subject and return the image with transparency.
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.lead: Separates the subject from its background and returns a transparent cutout of what is left.
alchemy.usecases.cut_out.body: The cut follows whatever the model takes to be the subject, so one clear subject cuts well and a crowd or a soft edge does not. The result carries an alpha channel, which is why it appears over a checkerboard in some viewers and over nothing at all in others.

alchemy.dev.flow.submit_desc: POST your source image and chosen forms to the async endpoint. You get back a request id.
alchemy.dev.flow.poll_desc: Poll the status endpoint with that id (this page polls every 10 seconds) until the overall state is 'done' and every form has reached a terminal state.

workers.what_are.title: What Are Workers?
workers.what_are.description: Workers are volunteer-run software that process AI generation requests for the Horde. They poll the [[gl:ai_horde|AI Horde]] API for pending [[gl:job|jobs]], generate results using your GPU, and return them to the requesting user. In return, you earn [[gl:kudos|kudos]], the Horde's priority currency.
workers.what_are.types_intro: There are three types of workers: [[gl:dreamer|Dreamers]] generate images, [[gl:scribe|Scribes]] produce text, and [[gl:alchemist|Alchemists]] handle post-processing tasks like upscaling and captioning. Each worker loads one or more [[gl:model|models]], the trained AI files that determine what it can generate.
workers.diagram.aria_label: Diagram showing how AI Horde workers process requests: a user submits a request to the API, a worker polls for and processes the job, then returns the result
workers.diagram.intro: AI Horde works as a request loop. Users talk to the API, and workers repeatedly poll the API for jobs they can run.
workers.diagram.loop_hint: This cycle repeats continuously — workers never accept inbound jobs, they always ask the API for the next one.
